class: An owner's rule wired into one route to a situation, while another route to the same situation stops
symptom: Mutual of Enumclaw (iCIMS), 29 September: the site took the owner's email, asked for the password and refused ATS_PASSWORD. The run logged LOGIN_REJECTED, stopped with the username and password as questions for the owner, and the owner asked why they were being asked when CLAUDE.md section 5 says what to do.
site: iCIMS; any employer site whose sign-in refuses the password of an account it knows
root_cause: The owner's rule -- reset a refused password to the same ATS_PASSWORD with the code emailed to the owner, once per site per run -- was reachable only from sign_in_to_existing_account, the route taken when a create form says 'an account already exists'. The sign-in route (account_state SIGN_IN -> handle_auth_gate -> attempt_auto_login) stopped at the refusal, and the account table sent every 'wrong password' page to the owner. The once-per-site limit lived in that one route's own set.
why_tests_missed: tests/test_existing_account.py tested the reset only through the 'account exists' route; tests/test_account_state.py asserted that WRONG_PASSWORD is always the owner's, encoding the gap as the expected behaviour.
fix: account_state decides it once: a refused password on an account the site knows (on record, or it took the email and asked for this account's password) and not yet reset on this site this run is RESET_PASSWORD; an unknown account, a second time, or a locked account stays the owner's. page_agent asks that table right after a refused attempt and when a page already shows the refusal, and calls browser_automation.recover_rejected_sign_in, which runs the existing reset with all its limits (employer sites only, emailed_codes.why_not, login_guard, no CAPTCHA, never a different password). The once-per-site limit moved into _reset_password_with_emailed_code, so both routes share it.
prevention: An owner's rule is written against the situation (a known account refused its password), in the one decision table, not against the page or route that first showed it; its limits live in the action itself so every route shares them. A test that asserts the owner must act is checked against the owner's written rules.
